title: Jaishankar Warns Gulf Situation Is Deep Concern in UAE Talks
excerpt: Meeting UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Mumbai, Jaishankar backed dialogue, unimpeded energy and trade flows, and noted bilateral trade has crossed $100 billion since the CEPA.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Mumbai on Tuesday that the situation in the Gulf remains a matter of "deep concern" for India.
  • Jaishankar said India will support all efforts to promote peace through dialogue and diplomacy, and backed the free, safe and unimpeded flow of trade, energy and fertiliser.
  • Bilateral trade has crossed $100 billion since India and the UAE signed the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement in 2022, Jaishankar said, with two-way investment still growing.
  • What this means for Indians in the UAE: Jaishankar publicly thanked the UAE leadership for ensuring the well-being of the Indian community there, putting community welfare on the formal agenda of the talks.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar held talks with the United Arab Emirates' Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Mumbai on Tuesday, telling him the situation in West Asia remains a matter of "deep concern" and that India will support all efforts to promote peace through dialogue and diplomacy.

Al Nahyan landed in Mumbai on Monday night on a two-day visit, according to The Hindu. His trip came amid a fresh wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia reportedly by Houthi militants, a development that has raised questions about security around energy infrastructure and shipping in the Gulf.

"The situation in the Gulf remains a matter of deep concern. We will continue to work together and support all efforts to promote dialogue and diplomacy."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister

In televised opening remarks, Jaishankar linked the regional discussion directly to trade and supplies. "We continue to support free, safe and unimpeded flow of trade, energy and fertiliser," he said. He also thanked his counterpart, and through him the UAE leadership, for ensuring the well-being of the Indian community in the UAE.

A partnership Jaishankar says is delivering

Jaishankar said the relationship is now living up to its promise as a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. In remarks reported by IANS, he said 2026 has been marked by an exceptional intensity of leadership-level engagement, citing the visit of UAE President Sheikh Mohammed to India in January, Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled leading the UAE delegation to the AI Impact Summit in February and to the 18th BRICS Summit, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's eighth visit to the UAE in May.

The economic figures were the centrepiece of his case. Despite global headwinds and regional challenges, Jaishankar said, the economic partnership continues to set new benchmarks. Bilateral trade has crossed the $100 billion mark since the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, and two-way investments continue to grow, reflecting the confidence of businesses in each other's economies.

The CEPA, signed in 2022, sits alongside a local currency settlement system and a bilateral investment treaty. The two countries are among each other's top trading and investment partners, and Tuesday's remarks extended the partnership beyond commerce. Cooperation in defence, energy and technology is acquiring a strategic character, Jaishankar said, people-to-people ties continue to enrich both communities, and the cultural partnership is gaining momentum.

Why the Gulf language matters

India's wording was measured but pointed. New Delhi did not name any party to the latest attacks in Jaishankar's opening remarks as reported, choosing instead to restate three positions: concern about the Gulf situation, support for dialogue and diplomacy, and support for unimpeded flows of trade, energy and fertiliser. For an economy that imports much of its energy through Gulf routes, disruption in the region feeds directly into fuel costs, freight rates and fertiliser supplies at home.

The UAE is also home to a large Indian community whose safety and welfare become an immediate diplomatic concern whenever fighting spreads in West Asia. Jaishankar's public thanks to the UAE leadership on that point signalled that community welfare was raised in the room, not left to consular channels.

What happens next

No new agreement or joint statement was announced in the reports of Tuesday's opening remarks. The test of the visit will be whether the trade, energy and investment initiatives the two sides reviewed move forward while the regional situation remains unsettled, and whether the language on dialogue translates into coordinated positions in multilateral forums. For now, both ministers presented the partnership as intact and expanding, even as the conflict on the UAE's doorstep gave the Mumbai meeting a sharper edge than a routine review would have carried.
